correctness.rationale: The single boundary kernel has unnormalized disk integral exactly 4. The pointwise triangle deficit for positive charges is nonnegative. Scaling \(z=\cos\delta+(\sin\delta)w\) maps poles to \(\pm i\) and factors the total deficit into \(|\sin\delta|\) times the same fixed integrand on a domain tending almost everywhere to the left half-plane. Near either pole the deficit is bounded by twice the other kernel, hence locally bounded; at infinity rationalization plus the \(O(|w|^{-1})\) relative phase gives \(O(|w|^{-3})\), integrable in two dimensions. Dominated convergence proves the two-sided cusp; a positive-area set with non-aligned nonzero summands proves positivity. Confocal elliptic coordinates correctly have Jacobian \((\cosh u-\cos v)(\cosh u+\cos v)\), yielding the positive integrand. Equal weights give the central-binomial identity by Tonelli and two explicit beta integrals, with summands \(O(m^{-5/2})\). Independent evaluation: 200,000-term series \(2.87108003758\), independent confocal midpoint integral \(2.87105782\) (quadrature approximation only).
correctness.risk: Weights must remain fixed and positive; full \(L^1\) limit rests on global dominator, not quadrature. No exact finite-angle or multiple-collision law is proved.

The exact weight-dependent half-plane coefficient and equal-charge convergent series give independently reusable mathematical data, not an arbitrary finite table.

final_claim: For fixed positive \(\alpha,\beta\), two charges at \(e^{\pm i\delta}\) in the unit circle have \(L^1\) Coulomb energy \(I_{\alpha,\beta}(\delta)=4(\alpha+\beta)-\mathcal C(\alpha,\beta)|\sin\delta|+o(|\sin\delta|)\), with a strictly positive integrable half-plane deficit and, for \(\alpha=\beta=1\), \(\mathcal C=\pi^2\sum_{m\ge1}b_m^2b_{m-1}/(2m-1)\), \(b_m=\binom{2m}{m}/4^m\).
limitations: Two fixed strictly positive real charges on the unit circle approaching collision only.
Unnormalized Lebesgue area; normalized area divides coefficients by pi.
Local asymptotic and exact equal-weight series; no finite-angle equality or multi-pole extension.
